listeningParts.title: Volunteering for a sleep study
listeningParts.contextDescription: A student phones a university research unit to volunteer for a study on sleep and memory.

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, Sleep Research Unit, Daniel speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, hi. I saw a poster in the student union about a study you're running, and I'm thinking of taking part. I was hoping you could tell me a bit more about it first.

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: Of course. The study is looking at how a lack of sleep affects memory. Volunteers spend two nights in our sleep laboratory. On the first night you sleep normally, and on the second night we wake you up several times. Each morning you do some short tests on a computer, mostly remembering words and pictures.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Right. And where exactly is the laboratory?

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: It's on the third floor of the Kingsley Building, which is the tall brick building next to the hospital car park. There's a lift, and our reception is straight ahead as you come out of it.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. Sorry to ask, but is it paid?

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: No need to apologise, everyone asks. Volunteers receive a hundred and twenty pounds for completing the whole study. If you have to leave early for any reason, we pay forty pounds for each night you've done. We also cover travel costs up to fifteen pounds, as long as you keep your tickets or receipts.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds fair. Are there any requirements?

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: A few. You need to be between eighteen and thirty-five, and in good general health. We can't accept anyone who works night shifts, because that disturbs the body clock and would affect the results. And we ask people not to have any coffee, tea, cola or energy drinks for twenty-four hours before each night in the lab.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hmm, that'll be the hardest part, to be honest. But I'm twenty-two and I'm a full-time student, so no night shifts.

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: Great. Then let me take some details. Could I have your full name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, it's Megan Thorley. That's T-H-O-R-L-E-Y.

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: Thank you, Megan. Now, we only run the study from Monday to Thursday. Which nights would suit you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I have lectures early on Tuesday mornings, so could I come on a Wednesday and Thursday? Next week, ideally.

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: Let me look. I'm afraid next Wednesday and Thursday are already full. The earliest I can offer is the following week: Wednesday the fourteenth and Thursday the fifteenth of March.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's fine, actually. I'd rather get it done before the exams start anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: Lovely. On both evenings, you'll need to arrive at eight thirty, so that we have time to prepare you before lights out at eleven. You'll get breakfast in the morning, and you should be free to leave by about nine.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And what do I need to bring?

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: Just your own pyjamas, a toothbrush and anything else you'd normally use in the morning. We provide the bedding, although some people like to bring their own pillow, which is fine. Please don't bring a laptop, though. We ask volunteers not to use screens for an hour before bed, so bring a book instead if you like to read.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: How do you actually measure the sleep? Is it uncomfortable?

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: Not at all. We attach small sensors to your head and face, which record the electrical activity of your brain and the movement of your eyes. They're held on with a special paste, which washes out easily with shampoo the next morning. There's also a camera in the room, but it's only there to check that you're safe.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's not too bad. One last thing: is there anywhere to park? I'll probably drive.

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.text: Yes, there's a car park directly behind the building. Normally you'd have to pay, but we'll send you a permit, so it's free for volunteers. Just leave it on the dashboard. I'll email that to you together with a short health questionnaire, which you need to complete before your first night.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Perfect. Thanks so much for your help, Daniel.

listeningParts.title: A garden for the senses
listeningParts.contextDescription: The manager of a sensory garden speaks to a group of visitors at the start of a tour.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Hartwell Sensory Garden. My name's Siobhan, and I've managed the garden for the last six years. Before you explore on your own, I'd like to give you a short introduction to what we do here and how the garden is laid out.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The garden was created twenty years ago by a group of parents whose children had visual impairments. They felt that ordinary parks were designed almost entirely for the eyes, and they wanted a place where their children could enjoy nature through touch, smell, sound and taste as well. Today, the garden is used by all kinds of people: schools, care homes for older people, people recovering from strokes, and families who simply like a quiet place to sit. In fact, about half our visitors have no disability at all. Many of them tell us that slowing down and paying attention to smells and sounds is the most relaxing part of their week.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The garden is run as a charity. We receive a small grant from the city council, but most of our income comes from donations, our café and the plant sales we hold every spring. We have only three paid staff, so we depend on around forty volunteers, who do everything from weeding to guiding school groups. If any of you would like to join them, there's an information leaflet at the entrance.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Everything here has been designed to be accessible. All the paths are wide and completely flat, so they're suitable for wheelchairs, and you'll notice that each path has a different surface: gravel, wood or smooth stone. That's deliberate. It means that people who can't see well can tell where they are from the feeling and the sound under their feet. Most of the plants are in raised beds, about knee height, so you can touch and smell them without bending down.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now, a few rules. Unlike in most gardens, you are encouraged to touch the plants here. The only exception is in the Scent Walk, where a few plants have red labels; those can irritate the skin, so please just smell them. And although we grow herbs and fruit, please only pick from the beds marked with a green sign, so that there's enough for everyone.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Let me tell you about the four areas. If you go left from here, you'll come to the Scent Walk. It's lined with lavender, roses and other fragrant plants. The best time to visit it is in the early evening, when many flowers release more of their scent. At the far end there's a herb bed, where you're welcome to pick a few leaves of mint or rosemary to take home.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Straight ahead is the Water Court. In the centre there's a fountain, which changes height every few minutes, so the sound keeps changing too. Around it is a shallow stream where children can put their hands in the water. It's also where you'll find our café, which serves drinks made with herbs from the garden.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: To the right is the Sound Garden. Here we've planted tall grasses and bamboo, which rustle in the slightest wind, and there are wooden and metal wind chimes hanging from the trees. Our most popular feature is a set of large outdoor drums, which anybody can play. We do ask you to keep the noise down after four o'clock, though, because that's when the garden holds relaxation sessions.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Finally, behind the Sound Garden is the Touch Wall. This is a long stone wall covered in plants with contrasting textures: soft, silvery leaves known as lamb's ears, spiky succulents, and mosses that feel like velvet. There are also carved stone panels showing animals, which visitors can explore with their hands. Our volunteers made the panels themselves, with help from a local sculptor.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: If you need anything during your visit, our volunteers are wearing yellow jackets. And if you'd like to learn more, we run workshops on designing sensory spaces at home on the first Saturday of every month. Enjoy your visit.

listeningParts.title: A presentation on flavour perception
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two psychology students, Priya and Tom, discuss their presentation on how we perceive flavour with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hi, Priya, Tom, come in. So, your presentation is on flavour perception, isn't it? How far have you got?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We've done most of the reading, and we've planned the structure. We wanted to check a few things with you before we start making the slides.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Fine. Talk me through the structure.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Well, we want to start with a misunderstanding that most of the audience will probably share: the idea that flavour is the same as taste. In everyday language people use the words interchangeably, but scientifically, taste is only what the tongue detects, and flavour combines taste with smell, texture, temperature and even sound.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. That's a strong opening. Are you going to mention the tongue map?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Yes, definitely. Lots of people learned at school that different parts of the tongue detect different tastes, sweet at the tip, bitter at the back and so on. But that's a myth. It came from a German paper published in 1901, which found only small differences in sensitivity, and it was later exaggerated in an American textbook. In fact, all five basic tastes can be detected across the whole tongue.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And the five are?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. We thought we'd say a little about umami, because people are less familiar with it. It was identified in 1908 by a Japanese chemist, Kikunae Ikeda, who was trying to work out why a soup made with seaweed tasted so good. He found that the taste came from glutamate.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Nice detail. What comes next?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: The role of smell. Most of what we call flavour actually comes from smell, but not from sniffing. When we chew and swallow, air carries smells from the back of the mouth up into the nose. It's called retronasal smell. That's why food seems tasteless when you have a cold.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: How are you going to show that? Demonstrations always work well.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We were going to ask volunteers to hold their noses and eat a jelly bean. They can usually tell it's sweet, but they can't identify the flavour until they let go of their nose. We've tried it on our flatmates and it works every time. One of them was convinced his was lemon until he let go, and it turned out to be pear.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a classic. Just check whether anyone in the audience has an allergy before you hand out sweets. And I'd keep it to three or four volunteers, otherwise it'll take too long.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Good point. After that, we want to look at the influence of the other senses. There's a well-known study from Bordeaux in which wine students were given a white wine that had been coloured red with a flavourless dye, and they described it using words normally used for red wine.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, I know that one. It's a good example of expectations shaping perception. Do you have something on sound?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We do. There's a study by researchers at Oxford in which people bit into crisps while wearing headphones. When the crunching sound was made louder, people rated the crisps as fresher and crisper, even though they were all identical.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Excellent. Now, my main concern is your conclusion. At the moment, from your plan, it just repeats the main points. I'd like you to think about practical applications.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Well, some hospitals are using this research to help elderly patients, who often lose their sense of smell and stop eating properly. And airlines are interested too, because food tastes different at altitude. Loud engine noise seems to reduce our sensitivity to sweet and salty flavours.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: That's interesting. We could finish with the hospital example, since it connects to health.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And one more thing: keep the text on your slides to a minimum. Use images and let your talk do the explaining.

listeningParts.title: How we hear
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a biology course on the structure of the ear and how hearing can be damaged and restored.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're turning to hearing, which is in some ways the most mechanical of our senses. I'll begin by tracing what happens to a sound as it travels through the ear, and then we'll look at how hearing is damaged and what can be done about it.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Sound is simply a series of pressure waves travelling through the air. The visible part of the ear, the outer ear, acts as a kind of funnel, collecting these waves and directing them down the ear canal. Its curved shape also changes sounds slightly depending on whether they come from above, below, in front or behind, which helps the brain work out where a sound is coming from.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: At the end of the canal is the eardrum, a thin membrane that vibrates when sound waves hit it. These vibrations are passed on to three tiny bones in the middle ear, often called the hammer, the anvil and the stirrup. The stirrup, by the way, is the smallest bone in the human body, only about three millimetres long. Together, these bones act as a lever, increasing the force of the vibrations. This matters because the inner ear is filled with fluid, and without this amplification most of the sound energy would simply bounce off the surface of the fluid, rather as your voice does when you shout at someone who is under water.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The inner ear contains the cochlea, which is coiled like a snail's shell. Inside it, running along its length, is a membrane lined with thousands of hair cells. When the fluid moves, the tiny hairs on top of these cells bend, and this bending opens channels in the cells, producing electrical signals. These signals travel along the auditory nerve to the brain, which interprets them as sound.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: What's remarkable is the way the cochlea separates different pitches. The membrane is narrow and stiff at the base of the cochlea and wider and more flexible at the top. High-frequency sounds make the base vibrate most, while low-frequency sounds travel further along and cause the greatest movement near the top. So, in effect, the cochlea works like a piano keyboard rolled into a spiral, with each position responding to a particular note.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now, the problem. Hair cells are delicate, and in humans and other mammals, once they are destroyed, they don't grow back. The most common causes of damage are ageing and loud noise. Exposure to very loud sounds, for example at concerts or from machinery, can bend or break the hairs, and repeated exposure causes permanent loss. Often the first cells to go are those at the base, so people tend to lose their ability to hear high frequencies first. Many people with noise damage also develop tinnitus, which is a ringing or buzzing sound in the ears that has no external source.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Interestingly, birds are able to regenerate their hair cells, and researchers are studying how they do this, in the hope of eventually triggering the same process in humans. For now, though, the main treatments are hearing aids, which simply make sounds louder, and cochlear implants for people with severe hearing loss.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: A cochlear implant works in a completely different way from a hearing aid. It bypasses the damaged hair cells altogether. A microphone worn behind the ear picks up sound, a processor converts it into a digital code, and this is sent to a thin wire of electrodes that a surgeon has inserted into the cochlea. The electrodes stimulate the auditory nerve directly. One of the pioneers of the modern multi-channel implant was Graeme Clark in Australia, whose team carried out its first implant operation in 1978.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Implants don't restore normal hearing. Users often describe the sound at first as robotic, and the brain has to learn to interpret it, which can take months of practice. But the results can be dramatic, especially in young children, who can learn spoken language if they receive an implant early. Next week, we'll look at balance, which, as you'll see, also depends on the inner ear.

readingPassages.title: The man with a hole in his head
paragraphs: On 13 September 1848, near the village of Cavendish in Vermont, a twenty-five-year-old railway foreman named Phineas Gage was preparing to blast away rock to make way for a new line. His job involved drilling a hole in the rock, filling it with gunpowder and then packing the powder down with a long iron rod, known as a tamping iron. At some point, probably while his attention was distracted, the iron struck the rock and produced a spark. The powder exploded, and the rod was driven upwards like a missile.

The tamping iron was just over a metre long, about three centimetres wide and weighed around six kilograms. It entered Gage's face below his left cheekbone, passed behind his left eye and left through the top of his skull, landing some twenty-five metres away. Astonishingly, Gage was not killed. According to witnesses, he may have been briefly unconscious, but within minutes he was talking, and he sat upright in an ox cart for the journey back to the town, where he climbed the stairs to his room at a local inn with little assistance.

Gage was treated by a local doctor, John Martyn Harlow, who cleaned the wound, removed fragments of bone and kept a careful record of his patient's condition. For several weeks Gage's survival was in doubt. He developed a serious infection, and at one point a coffin was made ready for him. Harlow drained an abscess and, by the end of the year, Gage was well enough to return to his parents' home in New Hampshire. He had lost the sight of his left eye, but his memory, speech and movement appeared to be largely intact.

What made Gage famous, however, was not simply that he had survived. In 1868, twenty years after the accident, Harlow published a report describing changes in his patient's character. Before the accident, Harlow wrote, Gage had been the most efficient and capable foreman in the company's employment, with a well-balanced mind. Afterwards, he had become impatient, rude and unable to stick to his plans, so much so that his employers would not give him his old job back. His friends, according to Harlow, said that he was 'no longer Gage'.

This account became one of the most cited cases in the history of brain science. At a time when many people still believed that the brain worked as a single unit, Gage seemed to show that a specific region, the frontal lobes, played a special role in personality, judgement and social behaviour. The case was used to support the idea of localisation, the theory that different parts of the brain are responsible for different functions, which gained ground later in the nineteenth century through the work of researchers such as Paul Broca.

Over time, however, the story was retold so often that it became distorted. Textbooks described Gage as a violent drunkard who wandered aimlessly for the rest of his life, claims for which there is little or no evidence. The Australian psychologist Malcolm Macmillan, who spent decades examining the original sources, pointed out that Gage in fact spent several years working as a stagecoach driver in Chile, a demanding job that required him to plan routes, handle horses and deal politely with passengers. Macmillan suggested that Gage may have made a considerable social recovery.

Our picture of Gage has also changed in another way. For more than a century, no photograph of him was known to exist. Then, in 2009, two collectors realised that an old portrait they owned, showing a man with a closed eye holding a metal rod, was in fact Gage. The image shows a smartly dressed, confident-looking man, quite different from the wild figure of popular legend. Researchers have also used scans of his skull, which is kept with the tamping iron at a medical museum at Harvard University, to reconstruct the path of the rod and estimate which areas of the brain were destroyed.

Gage died in San Francisco in 1860, after a series of seizures that were probably a long-term result of his injury. His case is still taught today, but increasingly as a lesson about evidence as well as about the brain. It shows how much a single dramatic example can shape scientific thinking, and how easily a story can grow in the retelling. It also points to a more hopeful idea that modern neuroscience has confirmed: that the brain is capable of significant adaptation, even after severe damage.

readingPassages.title: The map in the brain
paragraphs: Finding our way around is something most of us do every day without thinking about it. We leave home, walk to a bus stop, change to a train and arrive at work, and if a road is closed we can usually work out another route. Yet this everyday skill depends on one of the most sophisticated systems in the brain, and it is only in the last fifty years or so that scientists have begun to understand how it works.

For much of the early twentieth century, many psychologists believed that animals learned routes simply as chains of responses: turn left at the first corner, then right, and so on. In 1948, the American psychologist Edward Tolman challenged this view. He had observed that rats which had explored a maze could find shortcuts when their usual path was blocked, something a simple chain of responses could not explain. Tolman argued that the rats had formed what he called a 'cognitive map', an internal representation of the layout of their environment. However, he had no way of showing where or how such a map might exist in the brain.

The first clue came in 1971. John O'Keefe, an American-born scientist working at University College London, was recording the activity of individual nerve cells in the hippocampus of rats, a curved structure deep inside the brain. He noticed that certain cells became active only when the rat was in a particular part of its enclosure. One cell would fire when the animal was in one corner, another when it was near the centre. O'Keefe called them 'place cells', and he proposed that, together, they formed Tolman's cognitive map.

Over three decades later, in 2005, a further piece of the puzzle was found in Norway. May-Britt Moser and Edvard Moser, a married couple working in Trondheim, were studying an area next to the hippocampus called the entorhinal cortex. They discovered cells that fired not in one location but in many, and when the locations were marked on a plan of the enclosure, they formed a remarkably regular pattern of triangles, like the grid on a map. These 'grid cells' seemed to provide a coordinate system that allowed the brain to measure distance and direction. In 2014, O'Keefe and the Mosers shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their discoveries.

Research on humans has shown that experience can physically shape this system. In a famous study published in 2000, the neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire and her colleagues scanned the brains of London taxi drivers, who must pass a demanding examination known as the Knowledge, which requires them to memorise thousands of streets. The drivers had a larger rear section of the hippocampus than people who did not drive taxis, and the longer they had been driving, the larger it was. A later study followed trainees over several years and found that the growth appeared only in those who passed the examination, suggesting that the learning itself had caused the change.

The findings also have medical importance. The entorhinal cortex and the hippocampus are among the first regions to be affected in Alzheimer's disease, which may explain why getting lost in familiar places is often one of the earliest signs of the condition. Some researchers are now investigating whether simple navigation tests, carried out on tablets or in virtual reality, could help doctors identify people at risk years before memory problems become obvious.

Meanwhile, the spread of satellite navigation has raised a new question: what happens to these brain systems when we no longer use them? In a study at University College London in 2017, volunteers' brains were scanned while they navigated a simulation of the streets of Soho. When they planned their own routes, activity in the hippocampus increased whenever they entered a new street. When they simply followed instructions from a navigation system, that extra activity disappeared. The researchers were careful not to claim that sat-navs cause harm, but the study suggested that people who rely on them are giving the brain's mapping system less work to do.

None of this means that we should throw away our phones. Navigation apps have made travel easier and safer for millions of people. But some scientists suggest that it may be worth occasionally switching them off, studying a map before a journey or trying to find our way by landmarks. Like a muscle, the brain's inner map may benefit from regular exercise, and losing our way now and then may be a small price to pay for keeping it in good condition.

readingPassages.title: Can you train your brain?
paragraphs: Few ideas are as appealing as the promise that a few minutes of puzzles a day can make us sharper, protect us against memory loss and even delay dementia. Over the last two decades, this promise has supported a large industry. Smartphone apps and computer games that claim to train the brain have been downloaded by millions of people, many of them older adults anxious about their mental decline. The question is whether the science supports the marketing, and the answer, after many studies and a good deal of public argument, is considerably less encouraging than the advertisements suggest.

The boom began in Japan. In 2005, the games company Nintendo released a handheld game based on the work of the neuroscientist Ryuta Kawashima, who had argued that simple activities such as rapid arithmetic and reading aloud stimulated the brain. The game, which gave players a 'brain age', sold in enormous numbers around the world and inspired many imitators. Within a few years, online companies were offering subscription programmes promising improvements in memory, attention and problem-solving.

Few of these products had been tested properly. In 2010, a team led by the British neuroscientist Adrian Owen published one of the largest studies of brain training ever carried out. Working with a BBC science programme, the researchers recruited more than eleven thousand viewers, who trained online for several weeks using tasks designed to improve reasoning, memory and attention. The volunteers became steadily better at the tasks they practised. However, when they were tested on different tasks, they showed almost no improvement compared with a control group, who had simply spent the same time answering general knowledge questions online.

This distinction between near transfer and far transfer is central to the debate. Near transfer means getting better at the trained task or very similar ones; far transfer means improvements in general abilities that matter in everyday life, such as remembering appointments or managing money. Almost everyone agrees that practice produces near transfer: a person who plays a memory game every day will, unsurprisingly, become better at that game. The disagreement is about far transfer, which is what most brain-training companies imply in their advertising.

In 2014, a group of around seventy scientists organised by the Stanford Center on Longevity and the Max Planck Institute for Human Development issued a public statement warning that claims made for brain games were frequently exaggerated and sometimes misleading. Later that year, a larger group of researchers responded with an open letter of their own, arguing that some forms of training did produce meaningful benefits. Two years later, in 2016, the Federal Trade Commission in the United States reached a settlement with the company behind the popular Lumosity programme, which agreed to pay two million dollars over charges that it had advertised benefits it could not prove. In the same year, Daniel Simons and colleagues published an extensive review of the scientific literature, concluding that there was little evidence that training improved everyday cognitive performance.

Supporters of training often point to the ACTIVE study, a large trial of older adults in the United States that began in the 1990s. Participants who completed one particular kind of training, designed to increase the speed at which they processed visual information, were reported to have a lower risk of developing dementia ten years later. The finding attracted wide attention, but critics have noted that it was not one of the trial's original aims and that it needs to be confirmed by further research.

In my view, the most reasonable conclusion is not that brain training is worthless but that it has been badly oversold. Practising a task will make you better at that task, and for some people, such as patients recovering from brain injuries, carefully designed exercises may be genuinely helpful. But there is no strong evidence that playing a game on a phone will make the average person more intelligent, and it would be wrong for anyone to pay for an app in the belief that it will prevent dementia.

It is worth remembering, too, that the alternatives are often better supported. There is good evidence that regular physical exercise, sufficient sleep, social contact and controlling blood pressure all contribute to a healthy brain in later life. Learning a demanding real-world skill, such as a language or a musical instrument, may also offer more benefits than a game, because it combines memory, attention and social activity. I would argue that the best brain training may not look like brain training at all.
